newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK democrats say Tung won't soften on rights curbs.
newsitem.headline: HK democrats say Tung won't soften on rights curbs.

text.p: Hong Kong democrats said on Friday there was no sign the territory's future leader Tung Chee-hwa would retreat from planned curbs on civil rights, despite a string of assurances he has given to ease fears of repression.
Tung signalled this week that he is willing to clarify the wording of planned laws to restrict demonstrations and political groups after China takes over the territory on July 1.
Some newspapers portrayed his remarks as a softening, but his critics were highly skeptical and saw no retreat.

"I don't think he would back down even if the outcome of the public consultation is an overwhelming no," said Democratic Party politician Andrew To, who led a rowdy protest during a public meeting held by Tung's office on Wednesday.

To told Reuters that Tung and his aides Michael Suen and Henry Tang had made clear that only minor details would be altered after tapping public views -- not the basic principles of their planned changes to civil rights laws.
"I don't believe it's a concession," pro-democracy lawmaker Emily Lau said. If Tung was softening his stand, she said he should listen to the Hong Kong people and not change the two laws.
Independent political analyst Andy Ho said Tung would not budge from his plan to curb the right to protest and to ban foreign donations to local political groups.
"I don't see how Tung can go back to the laws that China's parliament has said must be repealed, so I don't know how it can be made more lenient," Ho said by telephone.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China as a quasi-autonomous region under a treaty allowing its capitalist system to continue for another 50 years.

The NPC, China's rubberstamp parliament, passed a resolution in March saying Hong Kong's Public Order Ordinance and Societies Ordinance must be repealed and replaced when Beijing takes over the territory of 6.4 million people from Britain on July 1.
Last week, Tung launched the curbs plan for "public consultation" to gather views on the changes.
Since then his popularity has fallen in the polls and he has been under fire from British Governor Chris Patten and the territory's pro-democracy camp.
In the past two days, Tung has hit back with two major speeches assuring people they would keep their freedoms under his rule.

"We are remarkably accommodating of different viewpoints, and tolerant of occasional aberrations from what is widely regarded as acceptable social behaviour. We wish to change none of this," he told a press awards function on Wednesday.

Tung said he would introduce a United Nations definition of "national security" into the new laws to dispel fears that the Chinese government would abuse its powers and have vocal critics and democracy activists jailed.
Hong Kong's former chief justice Yang Ti Liang, a member of Tung's inner cabinet, said changes would be made to wording in the laws to clarify concepts that aroused people's fears.
"I underestimated the public anxiety on this question... It's fine now that I have a fair idea of how the public feels. Let's look at it again," Yang told the South China Morning Post.
